steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper on the stability of manifold filters and manifold neural networks to deformations of the manifold. Explain the connection to graph filters and GNNs, introduce manifold filters and their frequency response, state the stability result and how it relates to prior bounds, discuss related work, and give the paper's organization.

steps.text:

- Frequency response of manifold filters
- Stability to deformations
- Related work and significance
- Organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Context
  - graph convolutional filters (cite), GNNs (cite): tool of choice for signal/information processing on graphs (cite examples)
  - graphs as samples of a manifold: explicit (point clouds, cite), implicit (wireless communication networks, cite)
  - graph convolutions/GNNs = discretizations of manifold counterparts; continuous insights -> discrete
- Main contribution
  - stability of manifold filters and manifold neural networks (MNNs) to smooth manifold deformations
  - first define manifold convolutional filters + frequency responses consistent with graph ones
- Manifold Filters
  - Laplace-Beltrami (LB) operator {\mathcal{L}}; manifold diffusion equation in auxiliary time t
  - initial condition f(x) -> u(x,t)=e^{-t{\mathcal{L}}}f(x), LB operator exponential (Section II-A)
  - filter {\tilde{h}}(t) acts on f(x): integral over time of {\tilde{h}}(t) times u(x,t) (Section II-B) [equation (1)]
  - recover graph filters by discretizing manifold and t (Section VI)
  - why: graph filters = linear combinations of graph diffusion sequence (cite); (1) = combinations of manifold diffusion sequence
  - generalize time convolutions: wave equation on real line, e^{-t\partial/\partial x} in (1) (Appendix A-F)
- Frequency response
  - definition [equation (2)]
  - motivation: manifold convolutions decompose on spectral components (Section II-C)
  - eigenfunction \bm{\phi}_{i}, eigenvalue \lambda_{i}; projections [\hat{f}]_{i}, [\hat{g}]_{i}; [\hat{g}]_{i}=\hat{h}(\lambda_{i})[\hat{f}]_{i} (Proposition 1)
  - generalizes time filter response: (2) is Laplace transform -> Fourier transform on imaginary axis \lambda=j\omega
  - generalizes graph filter response, a z-transform (cite)
- Stability to deformations
  - deformations = manifold diffeomorphisms; signal f on {\mathcal{M}}, f\circ\tau; same MNN \bm{\Phi}
  - \tau \epsilon -small and \epsilon -smooth -> outputs satisfy bound [equation (3)], given spectral properties of filters (Sections III and IV)
  - generalizes standard CNN bound (cite; diffeomorphisms of real line, filter banks, CNNs)
  - limit version of GNN bounds (cite) and related literature (cite)
  - as in those works: \hat{h}(\lambda) with decreasing variability as \lambda increases (Section III)
  - limited discrimination of high frequencies; multi-layer MNNs expected to beat filters when high frequencies matter (Section V)
- Related work and significance
  - focus on MNNs (limit of GNNs): existing GNN stability bounds grow with number of nodes (cite)
  - graphon neural networks (cite), graph models with variable sparsity (cite): size-independent results, like ours
  - manifolds: limit models for relatively sparse graphs, \epsilon -graphs and k -NN graphs (cite)
  - other random graph models for moderately sparse graphs (e.g., cite) lack manifold's physical interpretation
  - especially relevant: GNN transferability for graphs sampled from general topological space (cite)
- Organization: II (II-A preliminaries, II-B convolutions, II-C spectral); III filter stability, Theorem 1 additive + multiplicative LB perturbation, III-A, III-B; IV MNNs; V implications; VI discretization -> graph filters/GNNs; VII numerical examples; VIII conclusion; proofs in appendices

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Graph convolutional filters and graph neural networks (GNNs) have become the tool of choice for signal and information processing on graphs, see e.g.. In many applications the graphs can be considered as samples of a manifold. Sometimes this is quite explicit, like in the case of point clouds, and sometimes it is more implicit, like for wireless communication networks. In this context we can think of graph convolutions and GNNs as discretizations of their manifold counterparts. This matters because by studying continuous (manifold) signal processing we can often get valuable insights about discrete (graph) signal processing.

The main technical contribution of this paper is to analyze the stability of manifold filters and manifold neural networks (MNNs) to smooth deformations of the manifold. Before we develop the stability analysis we define manifold convolutional filters and frequency responses which are consistent with graph convolutional filters and frequency responses.

Manifold Filters. Consider a manifold with Laplace-Beltrami (LB) operator {\mathcal{L}} and write the corresponding manifold diffusion equation with respect to an auxiliary time variable t. For an initial condition f(x), manifold diffusions generate the time varying manifold function u(x,t)=e^{-t{\mathcal{L}}}f(x), where e^{-t{\mathcal{L}}} is the LB operator exponential (Section II-A). A manifold convolutional filter {\tilde{h}}(t) then acts on the function f(x) as the integral over time of the product of {\tilde{h}}(t) and the diffusion sequence u(x,t) (Section II-B),

A manifold convolutional filter is such that we can get graph filters back through discretization of the manifold and of the auxiliary time variable t (Section VI). The reason is that graph filters are linear combinations of the elements of the graph diffusion sequence and (1) defines manifold filters as linear combinations of the elements of the manifold diffusion sequence. Manifold filters are also generalizations of standard time convolutions. For this we need to consider the wave equation on the real line, so that the exponential of the derivative operator e^{-t\partial/\partial x} appears in (1) (Appendix A-F).

- Frequency response: definition (2); motivated by spectral decomposition (Section II-C)
  - eigenfunction \bm{\phi}_{i}, eigenvalue \lambda_{i}; projections [\hat{f}]_{i}, [\hat{g}]_{i}; [\hat{g}]_{i}=\hat{h}(\lambda_{i})[\hat{f}]_{i} (Proposition 1)
  - (2) Laplace transform -> Fourier transform on \lambda=j\omega; generalizes graph filter z-transform
- Stability to deformations: diffeomorphisms; f and f\circ\tau through same MNN \bm{\Phi}; \epsilon -small, \epsilon -smooth -> bound (3) (Sections III and IV)
  - generalizes CNN bound for real line; limit version of GNN bounds and related literature
  - needs \hat{h}(\lambda) with decreasing variability in \lambda (Section III); multi-layer MNNs vs filters for high frequencies (Section V)
- Related work: GNN stability bounds grow with number of nodes; graphons, variable sparsity; manifolds as limits of \epsilon -graphs and k -NN graphs; other sparse random graph models lack physical interpretation; transferability for graphs sampled from topological space
- Organization: Sections II–VIII, proofs in appendices

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Graph convolutional filters and graph neural networks (GNNs) have become the tool of choice for signal and information processing on graphs, see e.g.. In many applications the graphs can be considered as samples of a manifold. Sometimes this is quite explicit, like in the case of point clouds, and sometimes it is more implicit, like for wireless communication networks. In this context we can think of graph convolutions and GNNs as discretizations of their manifold counterparts. This matters because by studying continuous (manifold) signal processing we can often get valuable insights about discrete (graph) signal processing.

The main technical contribution of this paper is to analyze the stability of manifold filters and manifold neural networks (MNNs) to smooth deformations of the manifold. Before we develop the stability analysis we define manifold convolutional filters and frequency responses which are consistent with graph convolutional filters and frequency responses.

Manifold Filters. Consider a manifold with Laplace-Beltrami (LB) operator {\mathcal{L}} and write the corresponding manifold diffusion equation with respect to an auxiliary time variable t. For an initial condition f(x), manifold diffusions generate the time varying manifold function u(x,t)=e^{-t{\mathcal{L}}}f(x), where e^{-t{\mathcal{L}}} is the LB operator exponential (Section II-A). A manifold convolutional filter {\tilde{h}}(t) then acts on the function f(x) as the integral over time of the product of {\tilde{h}}(t) and the diffusion sequence u(x,t) (Section II-B),

A manifold convolutional filter is such that we can get graph filters back through discretization of the manifold and of the auxiliary time variable t (Section VI). The reason is that graph filters are linear combinations of the elements of the graph diffusion sequence and (1) defines manifold filters as linear combinations of the elements of the manifold diffusion sequence. Manifold filters are also generalizations of standard time convolutions. For this we need to consider the wave equation on the real line, so that the exponential of the derivative operator e^{-t\partial/\partial x} appears in (1) (Appendix A-F).

Frequency Response of Manifold Filters. We define the frequency response of a filter as

The motivation for this definition is that manifold convolutions can be decomposed on separate spectral components (Section II-C). Let \bm{\phi}_{i} be an eigenfunction of the LB operator with eigenvalue \lambda_{i}. If [\hat{f}]_{i}=\langle f,\bm{\phi}_{i}\rangle_{L^{2}({\mathcal{M}})} and [\hat{g}]_{i}=\langle g,\bm{\phi}_{i}\rangle_{L^{2}({\mathcal{M}})} are the projections of the functions f and g in (1) on this eigenfunction, then [\hat{g}]_{i} depends only on [\hat{f}]_{i} and we can write [\hat{g}]_{i}=\hat{h}(\lambda_{i})[\hat{f}]_{i} (Proposition 1).

This definition of the frequency response of a manifold filter generalizes the frequency response of a standard time filter. The reason is that the definition in (2) is a Laplace transform, and a Laplace transform reduces to the Fourier transform of the impulse response of a filter when it is restricted to the imaginary axis \lambda=j\omega. It also generalizes the frequency response of a graph filter, which is a z-transform.

Stability to Deformations. We show stability of manifold filters and MNNs with respect to domain deformations, which we formally define as manifold diffeomorphisms. We consider a signal f defined on a manifold {\mathcal{M}} and the signal f\circ\tau which is the composition of f with a diffeomorphism. The signals f and f\circ\tau are both passed through the same MNN \bm{\Phi}. In this paper we prove that if \tau is \epsilon -small and \epsilon -smooth then the MNN outputs satisfy

as long as the manifold filters in the layers of the MNN satisfy certain spectral properties (Sections III and IV).

The bound in (3) generalizes the standard convolutional neural network (CNN) bound from prior work, which studies diffeomorphisms of the real line and how they affect convolutional filter banks and CNNs. The bound is also a limit version of the GNN bounds of other prior work and the related literature. Like in all of these works, the bound in (3) holds when the frequency response \hat{h}(\lambda) of the filters in the layers of the MNN has decreasing variability as \lambda increases (Section III). So stability needs layers that have limited ability to discriminate high frequency components, and this means that we can expect multi-layered MNNs to do better than filters in learning tasks where high frequency components are important (Section V).

Related Work and Significance. We focus on stability analysis of MNNs, the limit version of GNNs, because all the existing GNN stability results have bounds that grow with the number of nodes in the graph. To get around this limitation, many works have studied neural networks on graphons and more general graph models with variable sparsity. The results in these settings don't depend on graph size, the same as the results for a limit object that we present here. Manifolds can give limit models for relatively sparse graphs, i.e. \epsilon -graphs and k -NN graphs. There are other random graph models that can model moderately sparse graphs (e.g., the variable sparsity models above), but these models don't have the physical interpretation of a manifold, and a manifold is often a better descriptor of real-world domains. Especially relevant to our paper is the work on GNN transferability for graphs sampled from a general topological space.

Organization. Section II introduces preliminary definitions (Section II-A), defines manifold convolutions (Section II-B), and introduces the spectral domain representation of manifold filters (Section II-C). Section III studies how stable manifold filters are to manifold deformations. It shows that a diffeomorphism gives a perturbation of the LB operator with additive and multiplicative terms (Theorem 1). Then it studies the effect on manifold filters of additive (Section III-A) and multiplicative (Section III-B) perturbations of the LB operator. Section IV extends the stability analysis of manifold filters to manifold neural networks, and Section V discusses what the results derived in Sections III and IV imply. Section VI explains how graph filters and GNNs are recovered from the discretization of a manifold. Section VII illustrates the results of Sections III and IV with numerical examples. Section VIII concludes the paper. Proofs are in the appendices.

Graph convolutional filters [1,2,3] and graph neural networks (GNNs) [4,5,6] have become the tool of choice for signal and information processing on graphs, e.g., [7,8,9,10]. In several applications, graphs can be considered as samples of a manifold. This is sometimes explicit, as in the case of, e.g., point clouds [11,12], and sometimes more implicit, as in the case of, e.g., wireless communication networks [7,8]. In this context we can think of convolutions on graphs and GNNs as discretizations of their manifold counterparts. This is important because valuable insights about discrete (graph) signal processing can often be gained by studying continuous (manifold) signal processing.

The main technical contribution of this paper is an analysis of the stability of manifold filters and manifold neural networks (MNNs) to smooth deformations of the manifold. Before developing the stability analyses, we define manifold convolutional filters and frequency responses that are consistent with graph convolutional filters and frequency responses.

Manifold Filters. Consider a manifold with Laplace-Beltrami (LB) operator {\mathcal{L}} and formulate the corresponding manifold diffusion equation with respect to an auxiliary time variable t. For initial condition f(x), manifold diffusions generate the time varying manifold function u(x,t)=e^{-t{\mathcal{L}}}f(x) in which e^{-t{\mathcal{L}}} is the LB operator exponential (Section II-A). A manifold convolutional filter {\tilde{h}}(t) then acts on the function f(x) as the integral over time of the product of {\tilde{h}}(t) with the diffusion sequence u(x,t) (Section II-B),

A manifold convolutional filter is such that graph filters can be recovered through discretization of the manifold and of the auxiliary time variable t (Section VI). The reason for this connection is that graph filters are linear combinations of the elements of the graph diffusion sequence [13,1,14], while (1) defines manifold filters as linear combinations of the elements of the manifold diffusion sequence. Manifold filters also generalize standard time convolutions. This requires considering the wave equation on the real line, so that the exponential of the derivative operator e^{-t\partial/\partial x} appears in (1) (Appendix A-F).

This definition is motivated by the fact that manifold convolutions can be decomposed on separate spectral components (Section II-C). Indeed, let \bm{\phi}_{i} be an eigenfunction of the LB operator associated with eigenvalue \lambda_{i}. If [\hat{f}]_{i}=\langle f,\bm{\phi}_{i}\rangle_{L^{2}({\mathcal{M}})} and [\hat{g}]_{i}=\langle g,\bm{\phi}_{i}\rangle_{L^{2}({\mathcal{M}})} are the projections of the functions f and g in (1) on this eigenfunction, [\hat{g}]_{i} depends only on [\hat{f}]_{i} and can be written as [\hat{g}]_{i}=\hat{h}(\lambda_{i})[\hat{f}]_{i} (Proposition 1).

This definition of the frequency response of a manifold filter generalizes the frequency response of a standard time filter, because the definition in (2) is a Laplace transform, which reduces to the Fourier transform of a filter’s impulse response when restricted to the imaginary axis \lambda=j\omega. It also generalizes the frequency response of a graph filter, which is a z-transform [15].

Stability to Deformations. We establish the stability of manifold filters and MNNs with respect to domain deformations, formally defined as manifold diffeomorphisms. We consider a signal f defined on a manifold {\mathcal{M}} and the signal f\circ\tau obtained by composing f with a diffeomorphism. The bound in (3) generalizes the standard convolutional neural network (CNN) bound in [16], which studies diffeomorphisms of the real line and their effect on convolutional filter banks and CNNs. It is also a limit version of the GNN bounds of [17] and related literature [18,19,20,21,22]. As in [16,17,18,19,20,21,22], the bound in (3) holds when the frequency response \hat{h}(\lambda) of the filters that make up the layers of the MNN has decreasing variability with increasing \lambda (Section III). Stability thus requires layers with limited ability to discriminate high frequency components, which implies that multi-layered MNNs can be expected to outperform filters in learning tasks in which high frequency components are important (Section V).

Related Work and Significance. We focus on the stability analysis of MNNs – the limit version of GNNs – because all existing GNN stability results have bounds that grow with the number of nodes in the graph [18,21]. To overcome this limitation, many works have studied neural networks on graphons [22,23,24] and more general graph models with variable sparsity [25]. Results in these settings are independent of graph size, as are the results for the limit object presented here. Manifolds can provide limit models for relatively sparse graphs, i.e. \epsilon -graphs and k -NN graphs [26]. Although other random graph models can model moderately sparse graphs (e.g., [25]), they lack the physical interpretation of a manifold, which is often a better descriptor of real-world domains. Of particular relevance to our paper is the work on GNN transferability for graphs sampled from a general topological space [27].

Organization. Section II introduces preliminary definitions (Section II-A), defines manifold convolutions (Section II-B), and introduces the spectral domain representation of manifold filters (Section II-C). Section III studies the stability of manifold filters to manifold deformations. It shows that a diffeomorphism results in a perturbation of the LB operator involving additive and multiplicative terms (Theorem 1), and then studies the effect on manifold filters of additive (Section III-A) and multiplicative (Section III-B) perturbations of the LB operator. Section IV extends the analysis of manifold filter stability to manifold neural networks, and Section V discusses the implications of the results derived in Sections III and IV. Section VI explains how to recover graph filters and GNNs from the discretization of a manifold. Section VII illustrates the results of Sections III and IV with numerical examples. Section VIII concludes the paper. Proofs are deferred to appendices.
